title: The Olympic Games: seven short texts
texts: The first Games we know of took place at Olympia, in southern Greece, probably from 776 BC, in honour of Zeus. Running, wrestling and chariot racing were the main events, and winners received a simple wreath of olive leaves rather than a medal. Cities at war agreed to a truce so that athletes could travel safely. The festival lasted more than a thousand years, until a Roman emperor banned it.

For fifteen centuries nobody competed at Olympia. Then a French educator, Pierre de Coubertin, argued that regular contests could build understanding between young people of different nations. In 1896 the first modern Games opened in Athens, with fourteen countries and about two hundred and forty athletes, all of them men. Women first took part four years later in Paris, though in far smaller numbers.

A visitor who has never read a word about the Games will still recognise several of their signs. Five linked rings stand for the union of the continents, and the flame, lit at Olympia with the sun's rays, is carried to the host city by thousands of runners. This relay began in 1936 and has become one of the most moving moments of the opening ceremony.

In 1924 the French town of Chamonix welcomed the first Winter Games, with skiing, skating, bobsleigh and ice hockey on the programme. The event was small at first but grew as new disciplines appeared. Snowboarding, for example, was introduced in 1998, although many people had seen it as a fashion rather than a serious sport. Today organisers need mountains, ice arenas and often more than one town.

In 1948 a doctor named Ludwig Guttmann organised a small sports competition at a hospital in Stoke Mandeville for soldiers injured in the war. Twelve years later, a similar event in Rome gathered around four hundred athletes and is now regarded as the first Paralympic Games. For many people, these athletes show that the limits of what is possible are set by attitudes, not by bodies.

Every bidding city promises a lasting benefit, and some deliver. Barcelona used the 1992 Games to rebuild its seafront, and East London gained a large park after 2012. Elsewhere, however, expensive stadiums have been left almost empty, and local taxpayers have paid for years. Supporters point to tourism and volunteers; critics reply that the final bill is almost always higher than predicted.

A festival that depends on television audiences cannot ignore the tastes of young viewers. That is why skateboarding, surfing and sport climbing joined the programme for Tokyo, and why breaking, a dance competition, appeared in Paris. Older fans sometimes complain, but organisers argue that new disciplines keep the Games alive. The list of events changes every few years, as it always has.
discuss: Do you think the Olympic Games are still relevant today? Why or why not?
Should new sports such as skateboarding or breaking be part of the Olympic programme?
Would your city benefit from hosting the Games? What would be the main advantages and disadvantages?
